newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea pledges further aid to North, seeks talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea pledges further aid to North, seeks talks.

text.p: South Korea on Friday announced additional food aid to North Korea, while its Red Cross organisation proposed the resumption of talks with its Northern counterpart next week on speeding delivery of relief supplies.

The South will contribute 50,000 tonnes of corn and 300 tonnes of powdered milk to North Korea to the United Nations in addition to a $6 million donation Seoul has made to the U.N. World Food Programme, a statement said.
The WFP has appealed for 200,000 tonnes of aid worth $98.5 million for North Korea, which is sliding into famine. The United States has pledged $25 million.
Meanwhile, the South Korean Red Cross proposed a meeting with the North Korean Red Cross either in Seoul, Pyongyang or at the border village of Panmunjom on May 23.

Kang Young-hoon, president of the South Korean Red Cross, sent a message to his North Korean counterpart via a telephone hotline at Panmunmjom to assure that the South would inform the North of the size of aid.
That issue led to a deadlock in the first inter-Korean Red Cross talks held in nearly five years on May 3 and 5 in Beijing.
The Beijing talks, held there at Pyongyang's insistence, stalled after the North demanded to know the exact amount of assistance.
The South wants to set up channels for direct relief deliveries rather than using the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies as a go-between.
The Southern Red Cross is due to deliver 3,600 tonnes of Chinese corn by train next week from China, the first batch of 15,000 tonnes donated by Southern civic groups to help stave off famine.
Scores of South Korean civic groups have said they are now campaigning to raise funds to buy a further 95,000 tonnes of corn to help relieve starvation by their compatriots in the North.

The South Korean government sent 150,000 tonnes of rice to North Korea in 1995 when floods devastated the Stalinist country's food crop, saying it hoped this would help lead to steps for detente on the Korean peninsula.
Pyongyang has spurned South Korean calls for bilateral government-level dialogue. Seoul is now ruling out any large- scale official aid to the North until Pyongyang accepts four-nation peace talks.

The peace talks, that would also involve the United States and China, are aimed at securing a lasting peace on the Korean peninsula by formally closing the book on the 1950-53 Korean War that ended in a truce.
